title: Harvesting Solid Carbon from Catalytic Methane Pyrolysis: Removal Routes, Catalyst Make-Up and Carbon Value: A Data-Driven Review
content: Catalytic methane pyrolysis forms no CO₂ directly and, by stoichiometry, makes 2.98 kg of solid carbon per kg of hydrogen; viability depends on removing the carbon, retaining the catalyst, selling the carbon and keeping it solid, because oxidizing all of it later would release 10.9 kg of CO₂ per kg of hydrogen, comparable to steam reforming. One acid wash of a 5 g sample retained 91–95% of the carbon with metal below the 50 ppm detection limit; carbon from bismuth-based melts carries 52–83 wt% metal unless salt-capped; gasification can restore catalyst activity, variably, but consumes the product. The longest reported operation exceeds 500 h cumulatively, in two moving-bed pilots. Published model estimates span $1.7–8.2 per kg of hydrogen without carbon sale and $0.8–4.1 with it (2023 USD); once-through catalyst make-up at the median laboratory carbon-to-catalyst ratio would add about $8.3. Reported emission intensities span 0–25 kg CO₂-eq per kg of hydrogen because boundaries, methane leakage, heat supply, and carbon credits differ; each 1% of upstream methane leakage adds at least 1.2 kg, and no assessment quantifies later oxidation of the carbon. We propose a design-for-harvest hypothesis map, a reporting checklist, data structures for machine learning, and emissions-accounting rules.
